assessment.nobel_worthiness: The quantum spin Hall effect and the Z2 classification opened the field of topological phases beyond the Landau paradigm. It is a clean, universal mechanism (protected edge states, bulk topology) that was predicted theoretically and then confirmed in transport. Its influence on condensed-matter physics, photonics and cold atoms is very large.
assessment.attribution: Kane and Mele identified the Z2 invariant and the spin Hall insulator. Molenkamp's group made the decisive HgTe experiment, following the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal, which is not in the supplied credit list. Hasan's three-dimensional topological insulator work is also decisive. With a three-person limit, the theory-plus-first-experiment split (Kane, Mele, Molenkamp) is the most defensible, and it leaves Hasan out. I cannot verify the allocation independently.
assessment.maturity: Strong. Multiple independent experimental confirmations exist across materials, and the interpretation has been stable for roughly two decades. Recognition is timely or somewhat overdue.
uncertainties: Allocation between Kane-Mele, the HgTe proposal and experiment, and the 3D topological insulator experiments (Hasan) is contested.
Part of the early credit (Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang, and Murakami) is outside the supplied names.
The surrounding Berry-phase and quantum Hall prizes (1985, 2016) may make this look partly recognised already.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The KPZ equation is a prime example of the surprisingly universal result in non-equilibrium statistical physics: a simple stochastic model with exact universality classes, links to random matrices (Tracy-Widom statistics) and a very wide reach, from growth and interfaces to directed polymers and quantum systems. Takeuchi's liquid-crystal experiments confirmed the exact distributions. This is the kind of understood, not merely observed, physics I value.
assessment.attribution: Kardar and Zhang (with Parisi, who is not in the supplied credit) formulated the equation; Takeuchi provided the decisive experimental confirmation. Exact solutions by mathematicians (Corwin, Quastel, Sasamoto-Spohn, Amir, and others) are not credited here, which complicates the allocation. Parisi's absence from the names is a notable gap, given he is already a laureate.
assessment.maturity: Theory is well established; experimental confirmation of Tracy-Widom statistics is reproducible but narrower. Recognition would be timely.
uncertainties: Whether a prize for the equation without Parisi, or without the exact-solution mathematicians, is fair.
Experimental confirmation rests on a few systems.
Real-world impact outside theory is limited and indirect.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The Bistritzer-MacDonald prediction of flat bands at magic angles and the discovery of correlated insulation and superconductivity in twisted bilayer graphene created the whole field of moire quantum matter. It is a tunable, simple platform for strongly correlated physics, and the theory-experiment pairing is neat.
assessment.attribution: Bistritzer and MacDonald made the theoretical prediction; Jarillo-Herrero's group made the decisive experiments (with Cao and Fatemi, who are not in the supplied credit). Credit for the experimental discovery involves junior researchers outside the list. The three-person set is otherwise coherent.
assessment.maturity: Strong replication across many groups, but the nature of the superconductivity, the correlated states and the role of strain and disorder are still debated. Possibly slightly early for the interpretation, though the discovery itself is secure.
uncertainties: The origin of superconductivity in twisted bilayer graphene is unresolved.
Credit to early experiment co-authors and to earlier theory (Lopes dos Santos, Peres, Castro Neto) is not captured by the supplied names.
Practical applications are still speculative.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The cavity method and its algorithmic descendants (survey propagation, belief propagation, message passing) are a central statistical-physics idea in disordered systems, constraint satisfaction, coding and high-dimensional inference. They connect directly to the statistical physics of learning that I teach. It is a strong example of one mechanism explaining many problems.
assessment.attribution: Mézard (with Parisi, a 2021 laureate not in the list) developed the cavity method; Mézard and Zecchina's survey propagation and statistical-physics view of random satisfiability is the main application work; Montanari's work on message passing and inference is more recent and mathematical. The three names cover related but different contributions, and the prize configuration would be hard to defend without Parisi's earlier recognition.
assessment.maturity: Mature in theory. Part of it is already recognised by the 2021 prize to Parisi. Further inference results are still developing.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2021 recognition of Parisi for spin-glass physics.
Whether this is one coherent discovery or several.
Experimental confirmation is indirect (algorithm performance, rigorous proofs).

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The jamming phase diagram offers a unifying picture of rigidity in disordered matter, with critical scaling, marginal stability and a link to glasses and granular matter. It is a clean, general statistical-physics concept and fits my taste for universal mechanisms in complex systems.
assessment.attribution: Liu and Nagel proposed the jamming phase diagram. Their key contributions are clear, but the later understanding of critical jamming (O'Hern, Silbert, Wyart, Parisi, Zamponi and others) was developed by others, so the scope of this prize is somewhat blurred.
assessment.maturity: The concept is accepted and tested by simulation and some granular experiments, but a complete theory of jamming remains incomplete. Might be somewhat early.
uncertainties: Whether the field has a complete theoretical picture.
Experimental confirmation is limited by what can be measured in granular systems.
Overlap with glass theory already recognised in other prizes.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Cold atoms in optical lattices realised the Hubbard model in a controlled setting, showing the superfluid-Mott transition, single-site imaging and Fermi-Hubbard physics. This gives quantum simulation of statistical-physics models with tunable parameters, and it is conceptually very close to my interests.
assessment.attribution: The Mott-insulator transition experiment (Greiner, Bloch), the Fermi-Hubbard realisation (Esslinger) and the theoretical proposal (Jaksch, Zoller, Cirac) are all central. Five names are credited here, and any set of three omits someone important, notably Zoller and Cirac, who proposed the scheme.
assessment.maturity: Mature and reproduced by many groups; the quantum-simulation program is still unfolding. Timing is reasonable.
uncertainties: Credit for the proposal (Jaksch, Zoller) versus the experiments, and for single-site microscopy.
The extent to which the simulations address open questions in condensed matter is still debated.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The experimental discovery of the Higgs boson by ATLAS and CMS confirmed the mechanism awarded to theorists in 2013, completed the Standard Model, and was an enormous collaborative achievement with unquestionable significance.
assessment.attribution: The discovery came from two collaborations of thousands. Credit to spokespersons and project leaders (Gianotti, Jenni, Della Negra, Virdee) is a social choice rather than a clean scientific attribution, and it does not fit the Nobel rule well. Jenni is omitted in my choice only because of the three-name limit, and I cannot argue that the choice is compelling.
assessment.maturity: Very mature; the Higgs properties have been measured to a few percent. It is possibly overdue, but the allocation problem has long been the obstacle.
uncertainties: How to credit large collaborations within the three-laureate limit.
Whether leadership roles correspond to decisive scientific contribution.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical lattice clocks, built on the magic-wavelength idea, reached about 1e-18 fractional precision. They enable tests of fundamental physics, relativistic geodesy and a possible redefinition of the second. The idea is simple and general and has strong experimental follow-through.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice clock and Ye's group delivered the most precise realisations. Both are well supported. Contributions of Hall, Hansch (frequency combs, 2005) and ion-clock work (Wineland, 2012) are already recognised, so the picture is not too cluttered.
assessment.maturity: Mature and strongly reproduced; routinely improved. Timely.
uncertainties: Whether the field is judged as an incremental extension of earlier prizes (frequency combs, ion clocks).
Magic-wavelength proposal credit may include others (Ye, Kimble, Takamoto) outside the supplied two names.
